findings.title: Canonical deployment exposes live Claude history on the LAN without authentication
findings.what: The runbook says the container reads live ~/.claude data, exports BIND_HOST=0.0.0.0 plus DASHBOARD_ALLOW_INSECURE_BIND=1, leaves DASHBOARD_USER/PASS unset, and calls this unauthenticated posture the canonical LAN deployment. Any peer able to reach the host can read the operator's private dashboard data over plaintext HTTP.
findings.fix: Make loopback the canonical posture. For any beyond-loopback bind, require DASHBOARD_USER and a strong DASHBOARD_PASS (and TLS via a documented reverse proxy); remove the insecure-bind export and describe the guard-disarming LAN mode only as prohibited legacy recovery guidance.
findings.acceptance: The canonical rerun cannot start a beyond-loopback deployment unless authentication is configured; following the documented LAN procedure yields an authentication challenge, unauthenticated requests cannot retrieve dashboard/history endpoints, and the documented URL uses TLS when traffic leaves the host.
findings.verifyNote: Second pass re-read the live-data, credential, canonical rerun, and decision sections at baseline. The document explicitly states that ~/.claude is mounted live, Basic auth is unset, and the guard is bypassed for LAN; this is not an inferred implementation mismatch.

findings.title: Shadow and replay flows lack a fail-closed guard against subscription-OAuth egress of Claude history
findings.what: The guide directs a background subagent to redo the same current task and replay agents to rerun past tasks, then sends results to an LLM judge. It provides consent and spend controls but no content classification, redaction, or exclusion for tasks containing ~/.claude-derived transcript/config content. Because these runs consume the Claude subscription windows, eligible history-derived prompts can be resent using the subscription OAuth credential, violating ADR 0008's absolute invariant.
findings.fix: Add an egress preflight before budget/consent that detects any ~/.claude-derived or secret-bearing task/context and skips it fail-closed. Permit analysis only through the registered, scrubbed, explicit Console-key path; document the skip reason and ensure judges receive only approved redacted fields.
findings.acceptance: A live or replay fixture containing a ~/.claude path, transcript excerpt, OAuth token, or derived history field is rejected before any subagent/judge request; an egress test proves zero subscription-OAuth request bodies contain such content, while a sanitized eligible task still runs.
findings.verifyNote: Second pass re-read the cited flow and baseline ADR 0008. ADR 0008:34-41 forbids subscription-OAuth transmission of ~/.claude-derived content and requires Console key, opt-in, registration, caps, and scrub for permitted analysis; ADR 0008:49-51 explicitly leaves the stricter shadow-calls rule untouched. The audited guide documents budget/consent but no data-egress gate.

findings.title: Proof documentation reports obsolete gate kinds
findings.what: The README says both former diff-gate pairs are now test-gated, yet the reproducibility table still labels `config-backed-flag-rename-diff` and `high-centrality-rename-diff` as diff gates. This makes the documented rerun design internally contradictory.
findings.fix: Change both table gate cells to `test` and remove or update the obsolete diff-gate disclosure at lines 87-88.
findings.acceptance: A text-level review finds no current claim that either renamed pair uses a diff gate, and the table identifies both as `test`.
findings.verifyNote: Adversarially re-read README.md:10-21, :73-88, and :118-129. The contradiction is current and internal to the audited document; manifest.json:295-298 and :455-458 additionally support that both structured gates are tests.

findings.title: Pair instructions promise a different objective gate than the manifest executes
findings.what: Both renamed-pair instructions state that `node check-diff.mjs` compares touched files with expected copies, while each pair's authoritative structured gate is `kind: test` with `node --test test.mjs`. A worker and reproducer therefore receive conflicting verification contracts from the same manifest.
findings.fix: Rewrite each stale title/instruction to describe its current multi-session test task and `node --test test.mjs` gate, or restore matching diff gates if that is the intended frozen design.
findings.acceptance: For every manifest pair, any gate named in `instruction` exactly matches `gate.kind`, `gate.command`, and the current chain task; specifically, neither renamed pair mentions `check-diff.mjs` while configured as a test gate.
findings.verifyNote: Adversarially re-read manifest.json:278-298 and :439-458 at the immutable baseline. README.md:20-21 confirms these are former diff gates now intentionally converted to tests, so the instruction text is stale rather than an alternate active gate.

findings.title: Generic SVG selector can falsely certify that sample data rendered
findings.what: The test claims to prove that each curated view rendered a populated table or chart, but DATA_SURFACE is `table tbody tr, svg`. Any SVG within main—including a PatternFly icon or other decorative UI graphic—makes the count positive. A parser or sample-shape regression that removes the primary chart can therefore pass while only incidental SVG remains, so the emitted evidence is not specific or reproducible evidence of the claimed data surface.
findings.fix: Replace the bare `svg` arm with a stable chart-specific locator or test attribute applied to actual populated chart roots; keep `table tbody tr` for populated tables and assert the matched element is outside empty-state/decorative UI containers.
findings.acceptance: For every DATA_VIEWS route, the test passes with its populated table/chart present and fails after replacing the primary data surface with an empty state while leaving ordinary SVG icons in main; the selector contains no unqualified `svg` arm.
findings.verifyNote: Adversarially re-read the detector definition and its sole assertion at baseline c8b98a29508b5eb7725c75a7e2a41dfa94c1feba. Lines 34-36 explicitly equate any SVG with a chart, and lines 91-95 require only a positive aggregate count; there is no chart ownership, data-bearing attribute, role, or decorative-SVG exclusion. The candidate is therefore a concrete false-negative in this file, independent of undocumented implementation details.

findings.title: GitHub CLI installer executes an unverified moving release
findings.where: .github/actions/ensure-gh/action.yml:26-33 resolves `releases/latest` and streams the selected archive directly into `tar` without a pinned version, digest, or signature check.
findings.what: A compromised upstream release, API response, or release asset can place attacker-controlled executables on PATH for subsequent workflow steps. The same workflow source can also install different binaries on different runs, defeating reproducible supply-chain review.
findings.fix: Pin an explicitly reviewed gh version and expected SHA-256 digest, download the archive to a file, verify it with `sha256sum -c`, and only then extract it.
findings.acceptance: A clean-run test shows the action downloads one fixed version, rejects an archive whose bytes do not match the committed digest, and never extracts before verification.
findings.verifyNote: Re-read lines 18-35 at detached HEAD c8b98a29508b5eb7725c75a7e2a41dfa94c1feba. The preinstalled-gh fast path does not protect runners where gh is absent; that path deterministically fetches `latest` and pipes the archive to tar with no integrity verification.

findings.title: Security-sensitive workflows execute actions through mutable tags
findings.where: The workflows use `actions/github-script@v7`, `anthropics/claude-code-action@v1`, `actions/checkout@v6`, `actions/setup-node@v6`, and `actions/upload-artifact@v7` rather than immutable commit SHAs.
findings.what: Owners of those action tags, or an attacker who compromises an upstream action, can retarget a tag and execute changed code with the workflows' tokens and secrets. The cross-review workflow is especially exposed because the Claude action receives `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` and a write-capable GitHub token.
findings.fix: Replace every external `uses:` tag with a reviewed full commit SHA, retaining the release tag only in an adjacent update comment; update SHAs through a controlled dependency-update process.
findings.acceptance: A static check over these three workflow files rejects every external `uses:` value that is not pinned to a 40-character commit SHA; workflow tests still pass with the selected SHAs.
findings.verifyNote: Re-read every cited `uses:` line at detached HEAD c8b98a29508b5eb7725c75a7e2a41dfa94c1feba and confirmed each external reference is a mutable major-version tag. The repository-local ensure-gh reference was not treated as an external tag.

findings.title: Author-vendor detector silently truncates PR commit evidence
findings.where: .github/workflows/agent-cross-review.yml:72-84 requests `pulls.listCommits` once with `per_page: 100` and classifies the joined result without pagination or a truncation guard.
findings.what: For a PR with more than 100 commits, qualifying co-author trailers after the first page are ignored. A mixed-vendor PR can therefore be classified as exclusively Claude or Codex instead of ambiguous, causing the wrong automated reviewer to run despite the workflow's stated evidence rule.
findings.fix: Use `github.paginate(github.rest.pulls.listCommits, ...)` to inspect all returned commits, or explicitly classify any PR whose complete evidence cannot be obtained as ambiguous.
findings.acceptance: A fixture or mocked API test with more than 100 commits and the only opposite-vendor trailer after commit 100 produces `ambiguous`; single-vendor trailers on later pages still produce the correct vendor.
findings.verifyNote: Re-read lines 67-85 at detached HEAD c8b98a29508b5eb7725c75a7e2a41dfa94c1feba. The call has `per_page: 100`, no page parameter, no `github.paginate`, and no total-count/truncation check, while classification immediately consumes that single response.

findings.what: These workflows invoke actions/checkout, actions/setup-node, and actions/upload-artifact through mutable major-version tags. findings.title: Stable publisher executes an unverified latest-version CLI archive
findings.where: The bootstrap step resolves the current latest gh release, streams its archive directly into tar, and places the extracted executable on GITHUB_PATH.
findings.what: The deployed tool version changes independently of this checkout, and the downloaded archive is neither checksum- nor signature-verified before its executable is used with GITHUB_TOKEN. TLS does not provide artifact immutability or release-asset integrity, so compromise or replacement of the upstream release path can become code execution in the stable publishing job.
findings.fix: Pin an explicit gh version and expected SHA-256 digest, download the archive to a temporary file, verify it with `sha256sum -c`, and only then extract and add its binary directory to GITHUB_PATH; alternatively use a reviewed SHA-pinned installer action with equivalent verification.
findings.acceptance: A controlled run succeeds with the pinned archive, then a test substituting an incorrect expected digest fails before extraction or execution; the workflow no longer queries `/releases/latest`.
findings.verifyNote: Re-read lines 54-66 at baseline: `set -euo pipefail` and `curl -f` cover transport/process failures but there is no digest, signature, immutable version, or verification step before the extracted binary is exposed for subsequent authenticated use.

findings.title: Untrusted pull-request code executes on self-hosted ARC runners
findings.what: Both workflows run for pull_request events on `arc-runner-set`, check out the pull request merge content, and then execute files controlled by that pull request. Even the preliminary docs-only jobs execute `scripts/ci-docs-only.mjs`; subsequent jobs run `npm ci` (including package lifecycle hooks), builds, tests, and other npm scripts. A malicious pull request can therefore execute arbitrary code on self-hosted runner infrastructure, potentially attacking runner persistence, accessible network services, or the surrounding cluster despite the read-only GitHub token.
findings.fix: Do not execute fork-controlled pull-request content on these self-hosted runners. Run pull-request validation on GitHub-hosted or equivalently isolated single-use runners with no sensitive network reach, or gate self-hosted execution to trusted same-repository branches after an explicit authorization step while ensuring the authorization logic itself runs trusted base-branch code.
findings.acceptance: Open a pull request from a fork that changes `scripts/ci-docs-only.mjs`, package lifecycle scripts, or an invoked npm script. Verify that no job executing the changed code is scheduled on `arc-runner-set`; trusted same-repository pull requests must still run the required checks on an appropriately isolated runner.
findings.verifyNote: A separate second pass re-read both event declarations, runner selections, checkout steps, and every execution step at baseline c8b98a29508b5eb7725c75a7e2a41dfa94c1feba. The trigger has no fork or trust restriction, and both workflows execute checked-out PR-controlled JavaScript before or during their main jobs. Read-only GitHub permissions reduce token impact but do not isolate the self-hosted host or network.

findings.title: Dispatch golden image installs an unversioned agent runtime
findings.what: The credential-bearing dispatch image uses mutable `node:24` and runs `npm install -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code` without a version or integrity lock. A rebuild can silently install newly published base or CLI code, which then runs alongside runtime OAuth credentials and session data.
findings.fix: Pin the Node base to an OCI digest and install an exact reviewed Claude Code version with verified npm integrity or from a locked artifact; update both pins only through reviewed changes.
findings.acceptance: The `FROM` instruction contains an `@sha256:` digest, the npm install target contains an exact version with integrity verification, and two clean builds from the same source resolve identical base and CLI artifacts.
findings.verifyNote: The separate adversarial pass re-read the complete file and confirmed the base has no digest, the npm package has no version or integrity constraint, and the comment claiming tag-based pinning is not enforced by the Dockerfile.

findings.title: Bootstrap script executes unverified mutable downloads as root
findings.what: The script fetches `latest` kind and kubebuilder executables plus a dynamically selected kubectl executable, marks them executable, and moves them into `/usr/local/bin` without checking a pinned version, checksum, or signature. A compromised redirect, release endpoint, or mutable upstream artifact becomes trusted executable code.
findings.fix: Pin explicit versions, download each artifact and its publisher-provided checksum or signature over HTTPS, verify it before chmod/move, and fail closed on any mismatch.
findings.acceptance: A static check confirms no `latest` or `stable.txt` selector remains and every downloaded executable is verified against a repository-pinned checksum or trusted signature before it is made executable or installed; a deliberately corrupted download makes the script exit nonzero.
findings.verifyNote: The adversarial re-read confirmed all three download-to-execution flows and found no verification command anywhere in the complete 23-line script.

findings.title: Operator image base layers are selected by mutable tags
findings.what: The builder uses `golang:1.25` and the runtime uses `gcr.io/distroless/static:nonroot`, both without immutable digests. Identical source builds can therefore consume different base contents, bypassing review and weakening provenance and rollback reproducibility.
findings.fix: Pin both `FROM` references to reviewed multi-architecture manifest digests while retaining human-readable version tags if desired.
findings.acceptance: Both `FROM` instructions include immutable `@sha256:` digests, and an image build records exactly those reviewed manifests for the intended platforms.
findings.verifyNote: A second full Dockerfile read at the specified baseline confirmed both `FROM` instructions are tag-only and that no later stage or configuration constrains their resolved digests.

findings.title: Devcontainer dependencies are not immutably pinned
findings.what: The Go image and both devcontainer features are referenced only by mutable tags. Recreating the environment can therefore fetch different publisher-controlled content without a reviewed repository change; the Docker-in-Docker feature has especially broad execution capability.
findings.fix: Pin the image and both feature references to reviewed immutable OCI digests, with an explicit update process for refreshing those digests.
findings.acceptance: Resolve each configured OCI reference twice and verify the file contains an explicit immutable digest for all three dependencies; rebuilding after tag movement must still select the reviewed manifests.
findings.verifyNote: A separate baseline re-read confirmed that lines 3, 5, and 6 contain tag-only references and no digest, checksum, signature policy, or other immutable resolution control.

findings.title: Downloaded operator tools are made executable without integrity verification
findings.what: The operator-sdk and opm bootstrap targets download release assets with curl and immediately chmod them executable. Neither path checks a pinned SHA-256 digest nor verifies a release signature, so a compromised release asset or delivery path becomes build-host code execution.
findings.fix: Pin an expected digest for every supported OS/architecture and verify the downloaded file with sha256sum -c before chmod/move; download to a temporary file and delete it on verification failure. Signature verification against a pinned trusted key is an acceptable alternative.
findings.acceptance: A bootstrap test using a corrupted or substituted payload must fail at the integrity-check step, leave no executable at $(OPERATOR_SDK) or $(OPM), and never invoke that payload; the authentic pinned payload must pass.
findings.verifyNote: Adversarially re-read probaitio-operator/Makefile:302-317 and :334-349 from the immutable baseline. Both pinned-version URLs flow directly from curl -sSLo to chmod +x with no checksum, signature, digest table, or verification command. The separate go-install-tool path uses Go module version resolution and is not cited as part of this finding.

findings.title: pull-secret prints the registry credential in command output
findings.what: The pull-secret recipe expands $(GHCR_PAT) directly into a recipe line that is not prefixed with @. Make therefore prints the expanded oc command before executing it, disclosing the registry PAT to terminal output and CI logs; the value is also supplied as a command-line argument.
findings.fix: Keep GHCR_PAT as a shell environment variable, suppress recipe echoing, and create the docker config Secret through a protected temporary file or standard input so the token is neither rendered by make nor placed in process arguments; ensure cleanup with a trap.
findings.acceptance: With GHCR_PAT set to a unique sentinel, a dry-run or mocked execution of pull-secret must create the intended Secret while the sentinel appears neither in captured stdout/stderr nor in the invoked command's argument list.
findings.verifyNote: Adversarially re-read probaitio-operator/Makefile:59-64 directly from baseline c8b98a29508b5eb7725c75a7e2a41dfa94c1feba. The recipe lacks @ and uses make-time $(GHCR_PAT) expansion in --docker-password, so make's normal recipe echo deterministically includes the credential. This is current executable configuration, not narrative or a fixture.

findings.title: DashboardInstance permits arbitrary code to run under the managed dashboard identity
findings.what: The image field accepts any string without an allowlist or digest constraint. A principal granted permission to create or update DashboardInstance objects can therefore select an attacker-controlled container image for the operator-managed Deployment, inheriting the managed pod's service-account identity and mounted credentials.
findings.fix: Remove per-CR image selection or enforce an admission-time allowlist of trusted registries/repositories and immutable digests. Use a minimally privileged service account for the resulting workload regardless.
findings.acceptance: The Kubernetes API rejects a DashboardInstance whose image is attacker.example/image:tag or any non-approved, non-digest reference, while accepting the approved digest-pinned dashboard image.
findings.verifyNote: The cited schema was re-read and contains only type:string. The smallest related baseline controller check confirmed that the reconciler copies this value directly into the managed Deployment rather than validating or replacing it.

findings.title: RemoteSession can turn an arbitrary namespace Secret into outbound Git credentials
findings.what: Both gitCredentialRef and repo accept unrestricted strings. The only stated repository-host enforcement occurs in the separate server-side dispatch path, so a principal allowed to create RemoteSession objects directly can bypass it, name an otherwise unreadable Secret, and cause its token to be used for a clone to an attacker-controlled host. This converts RemoteSession creation permission into a Secret-exfiltration primitive.
findings.fix: Enforce an HTTPS GitHub-host allowlist and an approved Secret-name policy at Kubernetes admission time, preferably with CRD CEL validations or a validating webhook; do not rely solely on the dispatch server. Bind credential references to explicitly authorized repositories.
findings.acceptance: A direct Kubernetes API request creating a RemoteSession with repo=https://attacker.example/repo and a populated gitCredentialRef is rejected before reconciliation, while an approved GitHub repository and approved credential reference are accepted.
findings.verifyNote: Adversarial re-read confirmed the CRD has no pattern, enum, CEL rule, or webhook enforcing either field. The smallest related baseline controller check confirmed that it mounts the named Secret and constructs the authenticated clone URL from these CR fields; shell quoting prevents command injection but does not prevent credential egress.

findings.title: Release workloads default to mutable container tags
findings.what: The session image, dashboard image, and operator manager image all default to or deploy :latest. Registry tag movement can therefore change privileged release workloads without a reviewed manifest change, preventing reproducible rollback and weakening supply-chain integrity.
findings.fix: Pin each release image by immutable sha256 digest, optionally retaining a human-readable version tag alongside the digest, and update those pins only through the reviewed release process.
findings.acceptance: Rendered release manifests and operator defaults contain no :latest references for the manager, dispatch, or dashboard workloads, and every selected image resolves through an explicit sha256 digest.
findings.verifyNote: A separate second pass re-read all three exact references at the immutable baseline. Each remains an active default or active Kustomize image rewrite; none is a commented example or overridden digest in the audited files.

findings.title: Default ingest endpoint sends session artifacts and bearer token over plaintext HTTP
findings.what: The default endpoint is `http://probaitio-dashboard.probaitio-system.svc`. The related baseline shipper passes the ingest bearer token in the Authorization header and uploads selected ~/.claude session-data artifacts to this URL, so any workload or network observer able to intercept in-cluster traffic can recover both sensitive session content and the reusable credential.
findings.fix: Terminate TLS at the dashboard ingest Service and change the default to an `https://` service URL, with the shipper configured to trust the issuing CA. Do not silently fall back to HTTP.
findings.acceptance: Render the default manager deployment and verify PROBAITIO_INGEST_URL begins with `https://`; then perform an ingest through the in-cluster Service using the configured CA and verify a plaintext HTTP listener cannot accept the bearer-authenticated artifact request.
findings.verifyNote: Adversarially re-read line 18 at baseline c8b98a29508b5eb7725c75a7e2a41dfa94c1feba and traced only the directly related baseline path: the manager propagates this value to the artifact-ship sidecar, which reads ~/.claude session-data, constructs an artifact body, and sends it with `Authorization: Bearer <PROBAITIO_INGEST_TOKEN>` using native fetch. The literal HTTP scheme therefore governs both payload and credential transport; this is not a comment-only, speculative, or stale claim.

findings.title: Metrics scrape sends a bearer token without authenticating the TLS peer
findings.what: The active ServiceMonitor sends the Prometheus pod's Kubernetes service-account bearer token but sets insecureSkipVerify: true. An intercepted or misdirected scrape can therefore disclose that token to an unauthenticated TLS peer. The secure TLS patch exists but is not enabled by the kustomization.
findings.fix: Enable monitor_tls_patch.yaml and its required cert-manager secret/replacements so the endpoint uses insecureSkipVerify: false with a verified CA and serverName; alternatively configure equivalent verified TLS without a client credential if bearer authentication is unnecessary.
findings.acceptance: Render the Prometheus kustomization and verify the ServiceMonitor endpoint has insecureSkipVerify: false, a populated CA reference and concrete service serverName, while an HTTPS scrape using the expected certificate succeeds and one using an untrusted certificate fails without receiving the bearer token.
findings.verifyNote: Second pass re-read the baseline: prometheus/kustomization.yaml actively includes monitor.yaml at line 2 while its TLS patch block is commented at lines 8-11; monitor.yaml reads the bearer token at line 16 and disables peer verification at line 23. The batch's monitor_tls_patch.yaml confirms a verified-TLS configuration exists but is not applied.

findings.title: Session identity can patch every pod in its namespace
findings.what: The dispatch Role grants get and patch on pods without resourceNames. Every workload using the bound dispatch ServiceAccount can therefore mutate labels and annotations on unrelated pods throughout the namespace. A compromised credential-bearing sidecar could interfere with selectors, policy controls, admission-driven behavior, or other pod-metadata consumers beyond its own session. The inline comment acknowledges that this is namespace-wide and defers confinement to future multi-tenant work, so the exposure is present in this baseline rather than speculative.
findings.fix: Remove namespace-wide pod patch permission. Have the trusted controller apply the claimed label, or create a per-session Role and RoleBinding after the generated pod name is known, with resourceNames containing only that pod.

The rule still has resources [pods], verbs [get, patch], and no resourceNames restriction; its own comment explicitly confirms namespace-wide scope. The adjacent Secret rule remains independently restricted to resourceNames [claude-oauth].

findings.title: Manager role has unused cluster-wide node-read privileges
findings.what: The operator ServiceAccount receives get/list/watch for every Node in the cluster. The directly related baseline reconciliation paths do not read, list, watch, or own Node objects, so this exposes cluster infrastructure metadata without a current operational need.

findings.title: Read-only RemoteSession role exposes session registration URLs
findings.what: The ClusterRole grants get/list/watch on complete RemoteSession resources. Baseline controller behavior stores the remote-environment registration URL in each resource's status, so users intended only to monitor resources can retrieve a claim-capable authentication URL. The separate status rule does not contain this exposure because Kubernetes get/list on the main resource returns status too.
findings.fix: Do not grant this viewer role access to RemoteSession objects until registration URLs are removed from CR status and stored behind a separately authorized mechanism; then expose only non-sensitive status fields to viewers.
findings.acceptance: Using Kubernetes impersonation for a subject bound only to this role, get/list/watch RemoteSessions must not return any registration or claim URL, while authorized session operators can still obtain it through the dedicated protected mechanism.
findings.verifyNote: An adversarial re-read of the immutable manifest confirmed all three main-resource read verbs. The directly related baseline status-writing code confirms that the full object carries the registration URL; removing only the status-subresource rule would therefore not fix the leak.

findings.title: Single-file batches bypass the body cap and synchronously amplify up to 64 MiB artifacts
findings.what: The cap is checked only when batch.length > 0. Consequently, a first raw file of up to 64 MiB is always accepted even though base64 expands it to about 85.3 MiB, above the default 50 MiB cap and the stated approximately 64 MiB endpoint limit. The process then retains the raw buffer, base64 string, JSON string, and synchronous gzip output, causing large peak memory use and event-loop blocking in the sidecar.
findings.fix: Enforce the encoded-size budget for the first item too, choose a raw-file ceiling derived from envelope and base64 overhead, and stream or chunk encoding/compression rather than materializing all representations simultaneously.
findings.acceptance: A test using a 64 MiB eligible artifact proves it is chunked or rejected before whole-file base64/JSON/gzip materialization; emitted request bodies remain below the configured cap including envelope overhead; and measured peak RSS/event-loop delay stays within an explicit sidecar budget.
findings.verifyNote: Adversarially re-read collection and serialization in the immutable baseline and re-derived the expansion: 64 MiB × 4/3 is approximately 85.3 MiB before JSON overhead. The batch-cap condition explicitly exempts the first file, after which JSON.stringify and gzipSync add further whole-body allocations.

findings.title: PoolHealthy reports claimed pods as warm
findings.what: The controller computes warm by excluding pods labeled claimed=true and persists that value in Status.WarmReady, but the PoolHealthy message uses len(running). Consequently, with one claimed running pod and poolSize=1, WarmReady is 0 while the condition claims "1/1 warm" and PoolHealthy=True. The status evidence is internally contradictory and can falsely report pool readiness.
findings.fix: Build the condition message from warm, and set PoolHealthy=True only when the required warm capacity is actually present; account explicitly for newly created pods if Pending is intended to count as warm capacity.
findings.acceptance: A reconciliation test with one claimed Running pod and poolSize=1 asserts WarmReady=0 and verifies that PoolHealthy does not report "1/1 warm" or PoolReady until an unclaimed replacement is observed in the pod list.
findings.verifyNote: The second pass re-derived the counters: running includes claimed Running/Pending pods at lines 69-74, warm excludes them, Status.WarmReady uses warm at line 173, but the condition claim uses len(running) at line 224. The contradiction is directly reproducible without relying on external documentation.

findings.title: RemoteSession can exfiltrate an arbitrary referenced Secret to a repository host
findings.what: Both GitCredentialRef and Repo come from the RemoteSession spec. The operator mounts the named Secret, reads its token, embeds it in a URL derived from Repo, and runs git clone. A caller permitted to create or update RemoteSession objects can therefore select another same-namespace Secret and an attacker-controlled HTTPS host, causing the operator-created pod to disclose that token during clone authentication.
findings.fix: Authorize GitCredentialRef against an operator-managed allowlist or dedicated credential binding, and validate Repo before mounting or reading the token so credentialed clones are limited to explicitly trusted HTTPS hosts. Prefer a credential helper that supplies credentials only after an exact host match instead of embedding the token in the URL.
findings.acceptance: A test constructs a RemoteSession with GitCredentialRef naming an unauthorized Secret and Repo set to an untrusted HTTPS host; reconciliation must reject it or build no pod containing that Secret. A second test proves an approved secret/host binding still clones without placing the token in the persisted remote URL.
findings.verifyNote: Adversarial re-read confirmed lines 167-175 mount the CR-selected Secret and lines 182-196 send its token through the CR-selected repository URL. Environment-variable quoting prevents shell injection but does not prevent credential disclosure to the selected network host.

findings.title: Metrics bearer token is written to test and pod logs
findings.what: The TokenRequest bearer token is interpolated into the kubectl --overrides argument. Run then writes the complete argument vector to GinkgoWriter and repeats it in returned errors. The pod also runs curl -v, which emits request headers, including Authorization, into pod logs that the test retrieves. Anyone with access to CI output can recover a live Kubernetes credential.
findings.fix: Use the curl pod's projected service-account token from a mounted file instead of placing a fetched token in kubectl arguments, remove curl -v, and make Run redact recognized credentials from both normal and error logging.

findings.title: Custom user installation path permits persistent shell command injection
findings.what: For `--user` with a custom directory, HOOK_PATH contains the caller-controlled absolute path. Validation rejects only double quotes and backslashes, then line 73 embeds the path inside a shell command stored in settings.json. A legal directory component such as `$(touch marker)` or a backtick substitution remains active inside the generated double-quoted shell word and executes whenever Stop or SessionEnd evaluates the registration, potentially with CLAUDE_HUB_TOKEN present.
findings.fix: Generate the registered command using robust shell argument quoting (for example, quote the literal custom path with `printf %q` while handling the intentional `$HOME` form structurally), and reject control characters; do not interpolate an untrusted path directly into shell source.
findings.acceptance: Install with `--user` into a temporary absolute directory whose literal name contains `$(touch <marker>)`, invoke the generated registration in an isolated environment, and assert that the marker is not created and the literal installed hook path is used. Repeat with a backtick-containing directory and verify settings.json remains valid JSON.
findings.verifyNote: Adversarial second pass re-read tools/cloud-capture/install.sh:41-73. Lines 44-55 preserve shell metacharacters from the custom path; lines 66-71 exclude only `"` and `\`; line 73 places the remaining value in executable double-quoted shell source. Inside double quotes, both `$()` and backticks still perform command substitution, so the claim is directly reproducible and is not mitigated by later JSON escaping.

findings.title: Credential-bearing CLAUDE_HUB_REMOTE is persisted in the cached Git configuration
findings.where: tools/cloud-capture/publish-claude.sh:814-820 accepts CLAUDE_HUB_REMOTE verbatim, while tools/cloud-capture/publish-claude.sh:354-356 writes REMOTE into origin.url.
findings.what: When CLAUDE_HUB_REMOTE is an HTTPS URL containing userinfo, such as https://token@example/repo.git, the secret is cloned with and then explicitly persisted in $HUB_DIR/.git/config. This contradicts the script's tokenless-remote policy and leaves a reusable credential at rest in the transcript cache.
findings.fix: Reject CLAUDE_HUB_REMOTE values containing URL userinfo, or parse credentials out and supply them only through the per-invocation credential helper while persisting a sanitized tokenless URL. Fail closed if the URL cannot be safely normalized.
findings.acceptance: Run the publisher with a credential-bearing CLAUDE_HUB_REMOTE against a disposable repository and assert it rejects the value or that `git -C "$HUB_DIR" config --get remote.origin.url` contains no password/token/userinfo; also confirm authenticated fetch and push still use only ephemeral credential injection.
findings.verifyNote: Adversarially re-read the credential helper at lines 258-269, clone/configuration path at lines 330-360, and target selection at lines 812-825 in the immutable baseline. The safe CLAUDE_HUB_REPO branch constructs a tokenless URL and enables ephemeral token auth, but the higher-priority CLAUDE_HUB_REMOTE branch bypasses that path and line 356 persists its exact value; no validation or sanitization intervenes.
